data: World cuisines, famous restaurants, and the techniques behind them.
Which Hollywood actor co-founded the Nobu restaurant empire with chef Nobuyuki Matsuhisa when the flagship New York location opened in 1994?

Robert De Niro partnered with chef Nobuyuki 'Nobu' Matsuhisa and producer Meir Teper to open Nobu New York in 1994, launching what became a global empire of over 50 restaurants (noburestaurants.com; Wikipedia: 'Nobu Matsuhisa').
Which Italian city is widely regarded as the birthplace of pizza, including the classic Margherita?

Modern pizza was born in Naples in the 1700s–1800s; the Margherita is traditionally said to have been created there in 1889 in honor of Queen Margherita of Savoy. Neapolitan 'pizzaiuolo' craft now holds UNESCO intangible cultural heritage status (Wikipedia: 'Neapolitan pizza'; UNESCO).
What name did Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda give in 1908 to the savory 'fifth taste' he identified in kombu seaweed broth?
In 1908 Kikunae Ikeda isolated glutamate from kombu and named the savory taste 'umami' ('pleasant savory taste'), now recognized as one of the five basic tastes (Wikipedia: 'Umami'; 'Kikunae Ikeda').
Which cooking technique involves briefly boiling food, then plunging it into ice water to halt the cooking?

Blanching scalds food in boiling water and then 'shocks' it in ice water to stop cooking, set color, and loosen skins — a standard prep step for vegetables (The Culinary Institute of America, 'The Professional Chef'; Wikipedia: 'Blanching (cooking)').
Ferran Adrià's avant-garde restaurant El Bulli was named World's Best Restaurant by Restaurant magazine a record five times. In which year did it permanently close?

El Bulli closed permanently in July 2011; Adrià transformed it into the elBulli Foundation, a creativity and innovation center based in Roses, Catalonia (elbullifoundation.com; Wikipedia: 'El Bulli').
Mole poblano, one of Mexico's most celebrated sauces, famously blends dried chiles with which unexpected ingredient?

Mole poblano combines dried chiles, spices, and nuts with a small amount of Mexican chocolate, which adds depth and a subtle bitterness rather than sweetness (Wikipedia: 'Mole poblano'; Diana Kennedy, 'The Cuisines of Mexico').
Which spice, harvested from the dried stigmas of a crocus flower, is the world's most expensive by weight and colors dishes like biryani and paella?
Saffron comes from the hand-picked stigmas of Crocus sativus — it takes roughly 150,000 flowers to yield a single kilogram, making it the most expensive spice by weight (Wikipedia: 'Saffron').
Which culinary technique creates a stable blend of two liquids that normally separate, as in mayonnaise and hollandaise?

Emulsification disperses one liquid (e.g. oil) within another (e.g. water or egg yolk) as tiny stabilized droplets; mayonnaise and hollandaise are classic emulsions held together by the lecithin in egg yolks (Harold McGee, 'On Food and Cooking'; Wikipedia: 'Emulsion').

Paul Bocuse held three Michelin stars for over 50 consecutive years. Which French president made the unconventional gesture of traveling to Bocuse's restaurant outside Lyon in 1975 to personally award him the Legion of Honour?

In February 1975, President Valéry Giscard d'Estaing dined at L'Auberge du Pont de Collonges to present Bocuse with the Legion of Honour — an unprecedented act that elevated the chef to a symbol of French national identity (Wikipedia: 'Paul Bocuse'; James Beard Foundation).
The Caesar salad is generally credited to restaurateur Caesar Cardini, who is said to have improvised it in 1924 — in which city?

Despite the name, the Caesar salad has no link to Julius Caesar: Italian-American restaurateur Caesar Cardini is widely credited with creating it at his restaurant in Tijuana, Mexico, in 1924, reportedly improvising from ingredients on hand during a busy Fourth of July rush (Wikipedia: 'Caesar salad').
British Food: God Save the Cuisine
A celebration of the United Kingdom's proudest culinary achievements — from chip butties to spotted dick.
The cooked breakfast featuring eggs, bacon, sausage, beans, and black pudding:
The Full English is also known as a 'fry-up' — because everything, somehow, ends up in the frying pan.
A 'chip butty' is a British sandwich filled with:
A chip butty is exactly what it sounds like: chips (fries) crammed into soft white bread, with optional ketchup.
The British pudding with a name that has made foreign menus awkward since 1850:
Spotted Dick is a steamed suet pudding with raisins — 'spotted' refers to the fruit and 'dick' likely derives from 'dough.'
Marmite, the British spread applied to toast that divides families, is made from:
Marmite is yeast extract and is famously polarising — its slogan 'Love it or hate it' is the most honest food advertising in history.
The dark, murky condiment called brown sauce slathered on bacon sandwiches contains:
Brown sauce like HP Sauce blends tamarind, tomatoes, and spices — best described as 'ketchup that gave up.'
The British 'meal' of canned baked beans poured over sliced white toast:
Beans on toast has been a perfectly acceptable British dinner since the 1920s, no shame required.
The lurid green side dish served alongside fish and chips at British chippies:
Mushy peas are dried marrowfat peas soaked and boiled into a vibrant green mush — the colour of ambition, the texture of regret.
Haggis, Scotland's beloved national dish, is traditionally cooked inside:
Haggis is oatmeal, onions, and sheep offal stuffed into a sheep's stomach and boiled — Scotland is very proud of this.
Coronation chicken, created in 1953 for Queen Elizabeth II, is cold chicken in:
Coronation chicken blends cold chicken with curried mayo and dried fruit — a royal invention that became a supermarket sandwich filling.
The British instant snack that once used 'the slag of all snacks' as its actual slogan:
Pot Noodle is a just-add-boiling-water instant noodle pot that embraced its trashy reputation in its own advertising.

Tropical orange-fleshed stone fruit, five letters:
Mango — five letters, fits the clue.

In the Navier–Stokes equations for incompressible viscous flow, the Reynolds-averaged closure problem arises because the momentum equations contain an unclosed term. Which tensor represents this term, and what physical phenomenon does it capture?
The viscous stress tensor τᵢⱼ = μ(∂uᵢ/∂xⱼ + ∂uⱼ/∂xᵢ), capturing molecular diffusion of momentum
The Reynolds stress tensor −ρ⟨u′ᵢu′ⱼ⟩, capturing momentum transport by turbulent velocity fluctuations
The strain-rate tensor Sᵢⱼ = ½(∂uᵢ/∂xⱼ + ∂uⱼ/∂xᵢ), capturing mean-flow deformation
The pressure-strain correlation Πᵢⱼ = p′(∂u′ᵢ/∂xⱼ + ∂u′ⱼ/∂xᵢ), capturing inter-component energy redistribution

Reynolds-averaging the Navier–Stokes equations introduces the Reynolds stress tensor −ρ⟨u′ᵢu′ⱼ⟩, a second-order symmetric tensor formed from the time-averaged product of turbulent velocity fluctuations u′ᵢ and u′ⱼ. It represents the rate of momentum transfer driven by turbulent eddies — analogous to viscous stress but arising from inertial, not molecular, mechanisms. Because this tensor introduces six new unknowns without additional equations, the system is unclosed; turbulence models (e.g., k–ε, k–ω, Reynolds-stress transport) exist specifically to approximate it.

Under France's Fifth Republic, which constitutional mechanism allows the President to bypass Parliament and submit legislation directly to a popular vote, and was used controversially by de Gaulle in 1962 to elect the President by direct universal suffrage — triggering a motion of censure that brought down the Pompidou government?

Article 11 of the 1958 Constitution allows the President to submit certain bills directly to referendum without parliamentary approval. De Gaulle's use of it in October 1962 to introduce direct election of the President was legally contested — critics argued Article 89 (the standard revision procedure) was required — but the referendum passed. The National Assembly responded by passing a motion of censure under Article 49-1, toppling Prime Minister Pompidou's government, though de Gaulle then dissolved the Assembly and won the subsequent elections.
Number of sides on a hexagon:
Hex- = six. Octagon has eight, pentagon has five.
The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture — one of the Millennium Prize Problems — asserts which relationship for an elliptic curve E over ℚ?
Every elliptic curve over ℚ is modular, i.e., arises from a weight-2 newform
The algebraic rank of E(ℚ) equals the order of vanishing of its L-function L(E, s) at s = 1
The group E(ℚ) is always finitely generated with torsion subgroup of order at most 12
For all primes p of good reduction, |E(𝔽ₚ)| = p + 1 − aₚ where |aₚ| ≤ 2√p

The BSD conjecture predicts that rank(E(ℚ)) = ord_{s=1} L(E, s). Choice A is the Modularity Theorem (proved by Wiles et al.). Choice C is the Mazur torsion theorem (proved). Choice D is the Hasse bound (proved) — it defines the trace of Frobenius aₚ but says nothing about the rank.
Rhode Island is about 1,545 square miles.
The yen has been Japan's currency since 1871.
Tallest mountain on Earth, measured from sea level:
Africa, Antarctica, Asia, Australia, Europe, North America, and South America.
From the 1992 inaugural season to today — how well do you know the EPL?
Who is the Premier League's all-time top scorer?
Alan Shearer scored 260 Premier League goals, mostly with Newcastle United.
Which club won the inaugural Premier League title in the 1992–93 season?
Manchester United, managed by Sir Alex Ferguson, won the first ever Premier League.
Erling Haaland joined Manchester City in 2022 from which club?
Haaland transferred from Borussia Dortmund and won the Golden Boot in his first PL season.
Which stadium is home to Liverpool FC?
Anfield has been Liverpool's home since 1892.
Who has won the most Premier League Golden Boots?
Both Henry and Shearer are tied
Thierry Henry and Alan Shearer are tied on four Golden Boots each.
Salah captains the Egyptian national team.
Brighton & Hove Albion, named for their coastal home.
Which player holds the record for most Premier League appearances?
Gareth Barry made 653 PL appearances across Aston Villa, Manchester City, Everton, and West Brom.
Which manager led Leicester City to their fairytale 2015–16 title?
Claudio Ranieri's Leicester won the title at 5000-1 preseason odds.
What is the largest stadium currently used in the Premier League by capacity?
Which club won four Premier League titles in a row from 2020–21 to 2023–24?
Manchester City's four consecutive titles is a PL record.
Newcastle United play their home games at:
St James' Park has been Newcastle's home since 1892.
Who is Arsenal's all-time leading goal scorer in the Premier League era?
Thierry Henry is Arsenal's all-time top scorer with 228 goals across all competitions.
In what year was the Premier League founded?
The Premier League was founded in February 1992.
Which goalkeeper has the most Premier League clean sheets all-time?
Petr Čech finished his career with 202 PL clean sheets, a league record.
Fog, hills, and Painted Ladies — how well do you know the City by the Bay?
Which San Francisco neighborhood was the epicenter of the 1967 'Summer of Love' counterculture movement?
Haight-Ashbury — the intersection of Haight and Ashbury streets — drew tens of thousands of young people during the 1967 Summer of Love (Wikipedia: 'Summer of Love').
Which neighborhood is historically known as San Francisco's 'Little Italy'?
North Beach has been the city's Italian-American enclave since the late 1800s, and still hosts the annual North Beach Festival (Wikipedia: 'North Beach, San Francisco').
Which San Francisco Bay island housed a federal penitentiary from 1934 to 1963?
Alcatraz operated as a federal maximum-security prison from 1934 to 1963 and is now managed by the National Park Service (nps.gov/alca; Wikipedia: 'Alcatraz Federal Penitentiary').
Coit Tower atop Telegraph Hill was funded by a 1929 bequest from which San Francisco socialite?
Lillie Hitchcock Coit left a third of her estate to the city 'for the purpose of adding to the beauty of San Francisco'; the tower opened in 1933 (Wikipedia: 'Coit Tower').
Which San Francisco bakery, founded in 1849, claims to be the city's original sourdough?
Boudin Bakery has baked sourdough in San Francisco since 1849 using a mother dough that traces back to its founding (boudinbakery.com/our-story; Wikipedia: 'Boudin Bakery').
Which seafood stew, created by Italian immigrant fishermen at Fisherman's Wharf in the late 1800s, is considered a San Francisco original?
Cioppino was developed by Ligurian fishermen working out of Fisherman's Wharf, combining the day's catch with tomato and wine (Wikipedia: 'Cioppino').
How many hairpin turns does Lombard Street's famously 'crookedest' block between Hyde and Leavenworth contain?
The one-block stretch of Lombard between Hyde and Leavenworth has eight tight switchback turns paved in red brick in 1922 to tame the block's 27% grade (Wikipedia: 'Lombard Street, San Francisco').
San Francisco's cable cars are pulled by an underground cable that moves at what constant speed?

All four cables run continuously beneath the streets at a constant 9.5 mph; cars start and stop when the gripman engages or releases a grip on the cable (SFMTA: 'Cable Car System'; Wikipedia: 'San Francisco cable car system').
Harvey Milk made history in 1977 when he was elected to which San Francisco governing body, becoming the first openly gay person elected to public office in California?

Milk won a seat on the San Francisco Board of Supervisors in November 1977 — San Francisco has no city council; the Board of Supervisors is its 11-member legislative body. He was assassinated alongside Mayor George Moscone the following year (Wikipedia: 'Harvey Milk').

In the aftermath of the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, Look Tin Eli and architects T. Paterson Ross and A.W. Burgren's deliberate exoticization of Chinatown's rebuilt streetscape (including pagoda roofs, dragon motifs, and ornamental tilework) served which historiographical phenomenon, later analyzed by scholars as both an act of community agency and a manifestation of broader American imperialism?
Urban renewal and the preservation of vernacular Chinese architectural traditions
Strategic commodification of ethnic difference through 'Oriental' aestheticization for tourism and capital accumulation
Intentional erasure of Chinese cultural memory through imitation of Beaux-Arts municipal design standards
Deliberate enforcement of segregation policies aligned with contemporary Progressive Era zoning theories

Scholars in ethnic history and urban studies (including works on the cultural politics of Chinatown reconstruction post-1906) have examined how Look Tin Eli's strategy of marketing Chinatown as an exotic tourist destination through deliberate architectural exoticization was simultaneously a pragmatic economic survival strategy against displacement and an internalization of Orientalist frameworks. This phenomenon—turning ethnic identity into commodified spectacle—reflects the complex tensions between self-determination and the dominant power structures of early-twentieth-century capitalism. The 'Oriental' aesthetic (pagoda roofs, dragon imagery, decorative tiles) was thus neither purely 'authentic' Chinese architecture nor purely imposed American design, but rather a negotiated, hybrid response to material constraints and cultural domination (studies on cultural commodification and ethnic heritage preservation).
Test your knowledge of epic ski destinations worldwide
In which U.S. state would you find the ski town of Aspen?
Aspen sits in the Rocky Mountains of central Colorado and comprises four mountains — Aspen Mountain, Aspen Highlands, Buttermilk, and Snowmass (Wikipedia: 'Aspen, Colorado').
Which season pass gives access to Vail, Whistler Blackcomb, Park City, and Breckenridge?
The Epic Pass, sold by Vail Resorts, covers its owned mountains including Vail, Whistler Blackcomb, Park City, and Breckenridge (epicpass.com; Wikipedia: 'Epic Pass').
The pyramid-shaped Matterhorn looms over which Swiss ski resort?
The car-free village of Zermatt sits directly beneath the 4,478 m Matterhorn (Monte Cervino) on the Swiss–Italian border (Wikipedia: 'Zermatt').
On a North American trail map, which symbol marks the easiest beginner runs?
North American resorts rate trails by symbol: green circle (easiest), blue square (intermediate), black diamond (advanced), and double black diamond (expert) (Wikipedia: 'Piste § North America').
Which British Columbia resort hosted the alpine skiing events of the 2010 Winter Olympics?
The 2010 Vancouver Winter Olympics held their alpine events at Whistler Creekside, on Whistler Mountain in British Columbia (Wikipedia: 'Alpine skiing at the 2010 Winter Olympics').
The resort town of Chamonix sits at the base of which mountain, the highest in the Alps?
Chamonix-Mont-Blanc lies beneath the 4,808 m Mont Blanc, the Alps' highest peak, and hosted the first Winter Olympics in 1924 (Wikipedia: 'Chamonix').
Which of these resorts is NOT on the Epic Pass?
Vail, Heavenly, and Stowe are all Vail Resorts mountains on the Epic Pass; Aspen Snowmass is an Ikon Pass destination owned by the Aspen Skiing Company (Wikipedia: 'Epic Pass', 'Ikon Pass').
The fearsome Hahnenkamm 'Streif' downhill, one of ski racing's most dangerous World Cup courses, is held in which Austrian town?
The Hahnenkamm races run each January on the Streif course above Kitzbühel, Austria — its near-vertical Mausefalle start is infamous on the World Cup circuit (Wikipedia: 'Hahnenkamm (Kitzbühel)').
A 'couloir' — like Jackson Hole's notorious Corbet's Couloir — refers to what kind of terrain?
A wide, gently groomed beginner slope
A steep, narrow gully running between rock walls
An artificial jump in a terrain park

A couloir is a steep, narrow gully flanked by rock. Corbet's Couloir at Jackson Hole, Wyoming, is entered via a mandatory drop-in and is one of North America's most famous expert lines (Wikipedia: 'Couloir', 'Corbet's Couloir').
Whistler Blackcomb has the greatest lift-served vertical drop in North America — roughly how much?
Blackcomb Mountain's vertical drop is about 5,280 ft (1,609 m) — a full mile — the largest of any resort in North America (Wikipedia: 'Whistler Blackcomb').
Which California resort hosted the 1960 Winter Olympics, the first Winter Games televised in the United States?

Squaw Valley, near Lake Tahoe, hosted the 1960 Winter Olympics — the first carried on U.S. television (by CBS). The resort was renamed Palisades Tahoe in 2021 (Wikipedia: '1960 Winter Olympics', 'Palisades Tahoe').
St. Moritz, the only town to host the Winter Olympics twice, lies in which Swiss Alpine region?
St. Moritz sits in the Engadin valley of canton Graubünden and hosted the Winter Olympics in 1928 and 1948 (Aosta Valley is in Italy, not Switzerland) (Wikipedia: 'St. Moritz').
